items.title: Archetypes of heat risk: An intersectional perspective on relative within-country differences
items.authors: Preinfalk E.; Beier J.; Hanger-Kopp S.; Bachner G.
items.source: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
items.keywords: Archetypes; Austria; Climate risk assessment; Heat risk; Intersectional vulnerability; Relative risk; Within-country differences
items.abstract: Climate risk is unevenly distributed across society, shaped by intersecting social, economic, and environmental factors. Existing risk assessments often fail to capture how these factors intersect to produce relative differences within countries, particularly under changing future conditions. We address this gap by developing a mixed-methods approach to operationalize intersectional vulnerability in climate risk assessments and quantify differentiated relative risk across a country's population. Applied in the context of heat risk in Austria, we combine qualitative insights from literature, stakeholder engagement and semi-structured interviews with quantitative clustering of georeferenced socioeconomic and heat exposure data. This allows us to identify five distinct heat risk archetypes that capture recurring patterns of exposure and intersectional vulnerability, revealing who is more at risk relative to others. Examples include blue-collar workers in urban low-income neighborhoods and elderly individuals whose vulnerability is compounded by low financial coping capacities. Extending the analysis into the future using climate projections and socioeconomic scenarios, we show that heat risk increases across all archetypes, driven not only by rising temperatures but also by demographic change and growing inequality. By integrating hazard, exposure and vulnerability within an intersectional and forward-looking framework, our novel approach enables a nuanced understanding of relative differences in heat risk within countries. The resulting archetypes can support the development and prioritization of effective and equitable adaptation strategies across scales that account for relative differences and changes in risk constellations until 2080. © 2026 The Authors.

llm.razonamiento: Aplicación parcial centrada en el método: operacionaliza la vulnerabilidad interseccional al calor en Austria mediante arquetipos que combinan edad, ingreso, ocupación y lugar, interpretados como posiciones conjuntas (I=1, IV=1), pero no teoriza estructuras de poder (II=0), apenas desarrolla justicia (V=0.5) y no reconoce agencia de los grupos afectados (VI=0).

ev.gate: Arquetipos como 'elderly individuals whose vulnerability is compounded by low financial coping capacities' combinan edad, ingreso y ocupación.
ev.I: Los arquetipos de riesgo por calor se interpretan como posiciones combinadas (p. ej., obreros de barrios urbanos de bajos ingresos).
ev.II: Atribuye el riesgo a exposición, demografía y creciente desigualdad, sin nombrar ni teorizar estructuras de poder.
ev.III: Diferencias relativas dentro de Austria, con escenarios hasta 2080; contexto socioespacial sin anclaje histórico-político.
ev.IV: Clustering georreferenciado de datos socioeconómicos y de exposición que operacionaliza la vulnerabilidad interseccional en arquetipos.
ev.V: Los arquetipos pueden apoyar estrategias de adaptación 'effective and equitable', sin desarrollar orientación transformadora.
ev.VI: Participan actores en entrevistas, pero los grupos en riesgo no aparecen como agentes.
ev.integracion: Integración parcial: identidades y método se articulan en los arquetipos, pero sin explicación estructural del riesgo.

items.title: CLASS CAPITALISM IN A POST-LIBERATION STATE: DEMOCRATIC SOUTH AFRICA’S BLACK DIAMONDS
items.keywords: class capitalism; elitism; elitism; intersectionality; patronage politics; politics; privilege; South Africa
items.abstract: Through its legislation fixed in its Constitution, South Africa has made great strides towards inclusion and equality for the marginalised. However, the gap between the rich and the poor has continued to widen. Elitism and privilege are as old as human existence and will continue in the future. This study will examine the political climate of class capitalism as a threat to human security. This article examines the impact of neo-liberal policy reform aimed at ensuring transformation and development, through an exploration of South Africa’s Broad Based Black Economic Empowerment (BBBEE) policies. Through its conceptual framework, intersectional theory explores hierarchy dominated by intersectional challenges that are connected to race, class, and gender and remain tied to power and privilege. Based on the findings of the study, South Africa’s post-liberation period instilled class divides that reinforced systems, processes and legacies of the past that still dominate the state and its people. Further, the study questions whether affluence and elitist politics create unequal distributions of resources, which contribute to human security threats within the region, including mass poverty, which impacts the lives of the vast majority of South Africans. There are clear winners and losers in South Africa as a result of capitalism and nationalistic discourses. It is confirmed in representations and categories across races, classes, and genders that exist in South Africa’s emerging class capitalism. In this paper, an intersectional study suggests that black African females remain highly stereotyped within hegemony, hierarchy, class, and social representations. © 2023 Author.

llm.motivo: Falla el criterio clima: 'the political climate of class capitalism' usa clima en sentido político; el objeto son las políticas BBBEE y el elitismo en Sudáfrica.
llm.razonamiento: No elegible: aplica teoría interseccional a raza, clase y género en Sudáfrica, pero el clima solo aparece como clima político, sin vínculo con el cambio climático.
